title: Docker Overview & Architecture
summary: What Docker is for, how the client talks to the daemon, and how registries, images and containers fit together.

blocks.text: Docker is an open platform to **develop, ship and run** applications. It packages an app into a **container**: a loosely isolated environment holding everything the app needs, so it doesn't depend on what the host has installed.

items: **Consistent delivery:** developers share containers, push them to test, and ship a fix by pushing an updated image. A good fit for CI/CD.
**Portability and scaling:** the same container runs on a laptop, physical or virtual machines in a data center, or a cloud provider.
**Density:** containers are lightweight, a cost-effective alternative to hypervisor-based virtual machines.

blocks.text: Docker uses a **client-server architecture**. The client sends requests; the daemon does the heavy lifting of building, running and distributing containers. They talk over a **REST API**, using UNIX sockets or a network interface, and may run on the same machine or the client can target a remote daemon.

rows: Listens for Docker API requests; manages images, containers, networks and volumes. Can talk to other daemons to manage Docker services.
Main way users interact. `docker run` is sent to `dockerd`, which carries it out. One client can talk to more than one daemon.
Another client, for apps made of a set of containers.
Mac/Windows/Linux app bundling `dockerd`, `docker`, Compose, Docker Content Trust, Kubernetes and Credential Helper.

blocks.text: The `docker` CLI does no work itself. It calls the Docker API, and `dockerd` executes the request.

rows: A **read-only template** with instructions for creating a container. Often based on another image plus customization. Built from a Dockerfile; each instruction creates a layer, and only changed layers are rebuilt.
A **runnable instance of an image**. Create, start, stop, move or delete it via the CLI or API; attach networks and storage, or make a new image from its current state.

blocks.text: A container is defined by its image plus the configuration given when it is created or started. When a container is removed, state changes not kept in persistent storage are lost.
Other Docker objects include networks, volumes and plugins.

items: Pulls `ubuntu` from the configured registry if it isn't local (like `docker pull ubuntu`).
Adds a **read-write filesystem** as the container's final layer.
Creates a network interface on the default network and assigns an IP address.
Starts the container and runs `/bin/bash`; `-i` and `-t` attach it interactively to your terminal.
Typing `exit` stops the container, but it **isn't removed**; you can start or remove it later.

blocks.text: **Under the hood:** Docker is written in Go and uses Linux kernel features. It creates a set of **namespaces** for each container; each aspect of the container runs in its own namespace, which limits its access.
A container is an **isolated process** with all the files it needs. Each app component (frontend, API, database) can run in its own container. Containers are:

items: **Self-contained:** no reliance on dependencies pre-installed on the host.
**Isolated:** minimal influence on the host and other containers.
**Independent:** deleting one doesn't affect the others.
**Portable:** runs the same on a dev machine, a data center or the cloud.

blocks.text: **Containers vs VMs:** a VM is a whole OS with its own kernel, drivers and programs. Containers **share the host kernel**, so more apps fit on less infrastructure. They are often combined: a cloud VM with a container runtime runs many containerized apps.

docker run -d -p 8080:80 docker/welcome-to-docker   # prints the full container ID
docker ps                      # running containers only
docker ps -a                   # include stopped containers
docker stop <the-container-id>

You don't need the full ID: enough leading characters to be unique works, e.g. `docker stop a1f`. If a container seems to be missing, check `docker ps -a`, because plain `docker ps` hides stopped ones.
A container image is a standardized package of all the files, binaries, libraries and configuration a container needs. Two principles:

items: **Images are immutable.** Once created they can't be modified; you make a new image or add changes on top.
**Images are made of layers.** Each layer is a set of filesystem changes (add, remove or modify files).

blocks.text: Docker Hub is the default place to find images. Its **Docker Official Images** (e.g. Redis, Memcached) are a curated set and a common starting point; other trusted content includes Docker Hardened Images, Verified Publishers and Docker-Sponsored Open Source.

docker search docker/welcome-to-docker
docker pull docker/welcome-to-docker          # no tag given: uses latest
docker image ls                                # SIZE is uncompressed
docker image history docker/welcome-to-docker  # add --no-trunc for full commands

An **image registry** is a central place to store and share images, public or private. **Docker Hub** is public and is the **default** registry. Alternatives include Amazon ECR, Azure ACR and Google GCR, or a self-hosted one such as Harbor, JFrog Artifactory or GitLab Container registry.

rows: The service that stores and manages images.
A collection of related images inside a registry, like a project folder (e.g. `project-a:v1.0`, `project-a:v2.0`).

blocks.text:
docker build -t <YOUR_DOCKER_USERNAME>/docker-quickstart .
docker tag <YOUR_DOCKER_USERNAME>/docker-quickstart <YOUR_DOCKER_USERNAME>/docker-quickstart:1.0
docker push <YOUR_DOCKER_USERNAME>/docker-quickstart:1.0
Don't forget the trailing `.` in `docker build`: it tells Docker where to find the Dockerfile.

flashcards.back: Client-server: the `docker` client sends requests to the Docker daemon (`dockerd`), which does the building, running and distributing.

flashcards.front: How do the Docker client and daemon communicate?
flashcards.back: Through a REST API, over UNIX sockets or a network interface.
Docker objects such as images, containers, networks and volumes. It listens for Docker API requests.

flashcards.front: Image vs container in one line each?
flashcards.back: Image: read-only template for creating containers. Container: a runnable instance of an image.

flashcards.front: What happens to a container's changes when the container is removed?
flashcards.back: Any state changes not stored in persistent storage disappear.

flashcards.front: Which Linux kernel feature gives a container its isolated workspace?
flashcards.back: Namespaces. Docker creates a set of namespaces for each container.

flashcards.front: After `docker run -i -t ubuntu /bin/bash`, you type `exit`. What state is the container in?
flashcards.back: Stopped but not removed. You can start it again or remove it.

flashcards.front: Key difference between a container and a VM?
flashcards.back: A VM runs a whole OS with its own kernel; containers are isolated processes that share the host's kernel.

flashcards.front: How do you list stopped containers too?
flashcards.back: `docker ps -a` (plain `docker ps` shows only running ones).

flashcards.front: Two core principles of container images?
flashcards.back: Images are immutable, and they are composed of layers (each a set of filesystem changes).

flashcards.front: Which command shows the layers of an image?
flashcards.back: `docker image history <image>` (add `--no-trunc` to see full commands).
A registry stores and manages images; a repository is a collection of related images inside a registry.
Docker Hub, a public registry anyone can use.

questions.stem: You type `docker run` in a terminal. Which component actually creates and starts the container?

options.explanation: The client sends the command to dockerd, which carries it out.
The client only sends requests through the Docker API.
Docker Hub is a registry that stores images; it doesn't run containers.
Compose is another client, for multi-container apps.

questions.stem: Which statements about the Docker client and daemon are true? Select 3.

options.text: They communicate using a REST API
options.explanation: The API runs over UNIX sockets or a network interface.

options.text: A client can connect to a remote daemon
options.explanation: They can be on the same system or the client can target a remote daemon.

options.text: One client can communicate with more than one daemon
options.explanation: The overview states this explicitly.

options.text: They must always run on the same machine
options.explanation: Remote daemons are supported.

questions.stem: Which best describes a Docker image?

options.text: A read-only template with instructions for creating a container
options.explanation: That is the overview's definition.

options.text: A runnable instance that you start and stop
options.explanation: That describes a container.

options.text: A service that stores and distributes images
options.explanation: That describes a registry.

options.text: The process that listens for API requests
options.explanation: That's the daemon, dockerd.

questions.stem: When a container is removed, changes to its state that weren't saved to persistent storage are lost.

options.explanation: The overview says such changes disappear on removal.
Only persistent storage survives removal.

questions.stem: You run `docker run -i -t ubuntu /bin/bash` on a host that has never pulled ubuntu, with default settings. What does Docker do? Select 3.

options.text: Pulls the ubuntu image from the configured registry
options.explanation: As if you had run docker pull ubuntu.

options.text: Adds a read-write filesystem as the container's final layer
options.explanation: This lets the container create or modify files.

options.text: Connects the container to the default network and assigns it an IP
options.explanation: No network options were given, so the default network is used.

options.text: Removes the container automatically when you type exit
options.explanation: The container stops but isn't removed.

questions.stem: Which technology does Docker use to give each container its isolated workspace?

options.explanation: Docker creates a set of namespaces per container.

options.text: A separate guest kernel per container
options.explanation: That's how VMs work; containers share the host kernel.
Content Trust is a component bundled with Docker Desktop, not the isolation mechanism.
The API is how the client talks to the daemon.

questions.stem: Why can a host fit more containers than VMs for the same apps?

options.text: Containers share the host kernel instead of each running a full OS
options.explanation: A VM carries its own kernel, drivers and programs.

options.text: Containers have no isolation at all
options.explanation: Containers are isolated processes.

options.text: Containers always run inside a VM
options.explanation: They can be combined with VMs, but that isn't required.
Containers can publish ports and join networks.

questions.stem: You started a container earlier, but it doesn't appear in `docker ps`. What should you run to check whether it exists but has stopped?

options.explanation: -a lists all containers, including stopped ones.
That lists images, not containers.
That searches Docker Hub for images.
That stops a running container.

questions.stem: To stop a container by ID you must type the full container ID.

options.explanation: Enough of the ID to be unique is sufficient, e.g. docker stop a1f.
A unique prefix of the ID works.

questions.stem: Which statements about container images are correct? Select 2.

options.text: Once created, an image can't be modified
options.explanation: Images are immutable; you build a new one or add on top.

options.text: Each layer is a set of filesystem changes
options.explanation: Layers add, remove or modify files.

options.text: Running a container edits the image's layers in place
options.explanation: Images are immutable; once created they can't be modified.

options.text: The SIZE shown by docker image ls is the download size
options.explanation: It's the uncompressed image size.

questions.stem: Which command lists an image's layers and the command that created each one?

options.explanation: It shows layers, sizes and the creating command.
That lists images, not their layers.
That searches Docker Hub.
That lists running containers.

questions.stem: Your team keeps `project-a:v1.0` and `project-a:v2.0` together on Docker Hub. What is the grouping that holds them called?

options.explanation: A repository is a collection of related images within a registry.
The registry (Docker Hub) holds many repositories.
A container is a running instance of an image.
A layer is a set of filesystem changes inside one image.

questions.stem: Docker Hub is the default registry, but you can also run a private registry.

options.explanation: Private registries can run locally or inside an organization, e.g. Harbor.
Registries can be public or private.
